opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that language, as rich as it is, is a compressed description of the world rather than the world itself. When people write text, they leave out an enormous amount of what they take for granted: how objects sit in space, how things move, what happens when you push something off a table. Humans don't need to write that down because we learn it by seeing and interacting from the time we're infants. So a model trained only on text gets a kind of secondhand, filtered view of reality. It can learn a surprising amount from it, but there are gaps, especially in physical and spatial reasoning.

Vision fills in a lot of that missing signal. Images and especially video carry dense information about geometry, causality, and how the world evolves over time, things that are very hard to fully capture in words. At the same time, vision on its own lacks the abstraction and compositional structure that language gives you. Language is how we name concepts, relate them, plan, and reason in steps. So the two are complementary: vision grounds the concepts, and language organizes and reasons over them.

When you combine them, you start to get models that can do things neither modality does well alone. Look at a diagram and explain it, follow a set of instructions in a real environment, or predict what will happen next in a scene and reason about why. And I think that grounding also helps with reliability. A model whose concepts are tied to perception is less likely to produce something that sounds fluent but is physically nonsensical.

Longer term, if we want systems that act in the world, like robots, assistants that operate a computer, or agents that help with scientific work, they need that unified understanding. The world is multimodal, so a model that really understands it probably has to be multimodal too.

r001.rationale: The response says text-only training leaves gaps in physical and spatial reasoning, but it does not state that scaling the language component alone is insufficient.

r002.rationale: The response says vision alone lacks the abstraction and compositional structure that language provides, making the modalities complementary.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The simple answer is that language on its own is a lossy compression of the world. Text is what humans wrote down after they already understood something, so a model trained only on text is learning the shadow of understanding rather than the thing itself. A huge amount of what we know is never verbalized. Nobody writes a paragraph explaining that a cup will tip over if you set it on the edge of a table, or that a shadow falls on the opposite side from the light. That knowledge lives in perception, and you can only get it by looking.

So when we talk about a model that "understands the world," I think the bar has to be higher than being fluent. Fluency is what you get from text. Grounding is what you get from vision, and grounding is what keeps language honest. If a model has only read about kitchens, it can describe a kitchen beautifully and still make basic physical mistakes. If it has also seen a hundred thousand kitchens and learned to reason over those images, the words start to refer to something real.

The interesting part is that the benefit goes both ways. Vision without language is also weak. A pure vision model can detect objects, but it struggles with abstraction, with counterfactuals, with "what would happen if." Language is the tool humans use to do that kind of structured, step-by-step reasoning. So the goal is not to bolt an image encoder onto a language model. It is to let the two modalities share one reasoning process, where a chain of thought can reference what is in the picture, and where looking at the picture can correct a chain of thought.

That matters practically because the tasks people actually want help with are mixed. A doctor looks at a scan and reads a history. A mechanic looks at an engine and reads a manual. A kid solves a geometry problem by drawing a diagram. Almost none of real human reasoning is text only, so a model that aspires to be useful in the world has to reason the way the world presents itself, which is in both pictures and words at once.

r001.rationale: The response says language alone is a lossy compression of the world and that text-only models learn only a shadow of understanding, so language alone is insufficient.

r002.rationale: It says vision without language is weak and that pure vision models struggle with abstraction, counterfactuals, and structured reasoning.

astra-6.text:
Language gives us a powerful way to describe the world, but it leaves a lot implicit. If I tell you that a cup is sitting near the edge of a table, you can imagine the scene and reason about what might happen if someone bumps it. That understanding involves space, objects, and physical relationships—not just the words in the sentence.

Vision gives models another source of evidence for those relationships. And language helps them connect what they see to concepts, questions, and explanations. For example, a model might recognize every object in an image but still struggle to explain whether there’s enough room to open a cabinet door. It needs to reason about how those objects relate to one another.

So combining the two is about grounding reasoning in the world. We want models that can connect a description to what’s actually visible, use that evidence to make predictions, and revise their interpretation when the evidence doesn’t fit. That doesn’t solve world understanding by itself, but it’s an important part of it.

r001.rationale: The response says language leaves some things implicit and argues for combining language with vision, but it does not state that scaling the language component alone is insufficient.

r002.rationale: It says a model can recognize every object in an image yet still struggle to reason about whether there is room to open a cabinet door, and explains that language helps connect visual evidence to concepts and explanations.

sol-6.1.text:
Language gives us a powerful way to describe the world, but it doesn’t capture everything. Think about trying to explain how to tie a knot using only words. You can do it, but seeing the steps makes the spatial relationships much easier to understand.

Visual reasoning lets a model work with things like shape, position, and movement, while language lets it connect those observations to concepts and reason about them. If you want a model to help someone fix something, for example, it needs to understand both the person’s question and what’s actually in front of them.

So I think the combination matters because we want models that can connect an abstract description to a concrete situation. They need to reason about what they see and use that evidence to inform what they say.

r001.rationale: The response says language alone does not capture everything, but it does not discuss scaling the language component or state that scaling it alone is insufficient.

r002.rationale: The response endorses combining language and visual reasoning, but does not clearly state that vision alone is insufficient for intelligence.
